narrative:
The model determined that you have a 66.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. First, your LSAT score of 38 was the strongest influence, and it worked in your favor by pushing the prediction toward passing. Second, your class ranking at the end of your third year pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were admitted. Third, your first-year class ranking also pushed toward failure. Again, you stood in the second decile while admitted students averaged around the sixth.

Taken together, the two weaker academic rankings outweighed the positive signal from your LSAT and led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. Your family income, undergraduate GPA, full-time status, gender, and race played little or no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it meaningfully. Many students successfully reapply after boosting these key areas.
